speechtext: Is the right hon. the Prime Minister in a position to state approximately when the recent report of the Imperial conference will be submitted to the House for consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Tuesday, of
next week, on the orders of the day, might be an appropriate time at which to take up the proceedings of the Imperial conference. As to procedure, the government has thought it would probably suit the convenience of the House if, on motion to go into supply, a statement were made with respect to the Imperial conference proceedings and hon. members could speak with reference thereto
Imperial Conference

before the Speaker leaves the chair. Thereafter we would go into supply, on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, at which time incidental matters could be taken up more in detail. I think it would be advisable to adopt the procedure I have mentioned.
Is it not the intention of the government to submit to the House a resolution approving of the terms of the Imperial conference report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In this respect the government intends to follow the example of the parliament at Westminster, an example which I think has been followed by the parliaments of the various dominions, including this country, on former occasions. There has not been, except with reference to a specific part of any report, any formal resolution in regard to the proceedings. The government therefore does not propose to bring in any formal resolution with regard to the proceedings as a whole. If any hon. member wishes to introduce a formal resolution either approving of or taking exception to any feature of the report of the conference he is of course, at liberty to do so.
Will that be on an amendment to the motion to go into supply?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: An amendment can if desired be moved at that time; on the motion to go into supply an amendment can be made, as the hon. member knows. It is for each hon. member for himself to decide the time at which he shall bring in a motion and what form it shall take.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have just
said the procedure in all the parliaments in the empire is identical on this respect. The government of Great Britain has not submitted to the British parliament a formal resolution with respect to the conference; neither have the governments of Australia, South Africa, New Zealand or any other country. With respect to the present report we do not propose to adopt a course of procedure different from that adopted by the other parts of the empire.

After the conference of

in respect to the treaty-making power, or the manner in which the treaty should be signed, the work of the conference, and we expressly ratified it in this House by resolution. Mr. Chairman, in regard
to the schedule, I pointed out before the railway committee that the cost of this piece of construction is exceedingly heavy. It will be noted that this branch line of 7.9 miles in length is to cost $1,683,000, or $213,038 per mile. I am advised that the nature of the country is not such as to warrant this heavy expenditure. However, it was pointed out in the railway committee that this exceedingly high cost was largely due to certain very heavy fills and cuts. The objection I took there was that the improvement is of the nature of a final or permanent improvement to a railway which might be considered as of finished character and in first-class financial condition, and is not warranted in connection with a railway that essentially should be built as economically as possible. Therefore
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

my position before the railway committee was that this expenditure is unjustifiable at this time, that the company might well expend the $1,600,000 on much more needed work elsewhere, and that this particular type of ultimate improvement could wait until the railway is in better financial condition. Furthermore, I would point out that if a three-mile section of the Canadian Pacific is used the balance of this branch line, namely, 4.8 miles, will cost $1,327,000 or about $270,000 per mile. Some of us who have followed railway construction bills through parliament for many years believe this to be the highest cost per mile proposed in any charter that has gone through this House. Personally I consider it an exorbitant charge and one which is unjustifiable under present conditions.

My hon. friend expresses now the same views he gave in the committee. I can only put forward in answer to him the statement of the responsible officers of the road as to the immediate advantage to be gained by making this improvement, which will bring its own immediate justification. The hon. member takes the view that such an improvement as this cut-off would be justified only in connection with a road which is complete and in excellent financial condition. The officials of the railway, on the other hand, demonstrate that they can by means of this expenditure double their trainload behind the engine and thereby substantially reduce operating costs. They are satisfied, and they have demonstrated to my satisfaction, that this expenditure will immediately return more than 12 per cent upon the outlay in the way of reduced operating costs, and will increase the volume of business over the territory affected. That is my only justification for the proposed expenditure and my only answer to the criticism of the hon. gentleman. We regard this as an improvement of the kind that should constantly be made on the Canadian National lines-that is, an improvement in connection with which it can be demonstrated that the returns in reduced cost of operation will more than pay interest on the money spent.

A good many members are not on the committee and would like some information as to why the cost of constructing this seven miles is so enormous. It has been stated that this projected work will cost more than any other seven miles of railway in Canada.
I do not know that that is true.

It has been so stated. I should like the minister to gratify my curiosity by giving me some information explaining why the road should cost between two hundred and three hundred thousand dollars a mile to construct. The country is not difficult. The Canadian Pacific Railway has constructed a line through practically the same country and the cost of operation in this case is not anything like the amount proposed in this bill; it would not be more than a quarter of it. Again I would ask for an explanation of the expenditure of this enormous sum of money on so short a line of road.

I cannot check the accuracy of my hon. friend's statement regarding the cost of the Canadian Pacific Railway line in the territory. I trust he will supply me with precise information in that regard, if he has it, because it will be of assistance to me in judging whether or not the permanent officials of the Canadian National are correct in their presentation to me. With regard to the general question, the present grade on the main line is 1.5 per cent, and this work will reduce it to six-tenths of one per cent. The road was built in its present location because, as is often the case, it would have cost too much money at the time of its construction to produce a six-tenth grade. The hill, therefore, was climbed. The chief engineer of the Canadian National Railways informed the committee the other day that the cost of the work was almost altogether due to heavy cut and fill, with banks in the neighbourhood of fifty feet high on a portion of the construction. The minister, I know, is aware of it from the way he spoke. The minister has had the matter under consideration on more than one occasion, but apparently he has yielded to pressure from those whom my hon. friend would describe as capitalists, and now proposes to capitalize this amount instead of allowing it to be charged against operating revenues. A very important principle is involved in that connection. If you have a surplus of a million and can carry out needed improvements to the extent of $S00,000 without borrowing money, and have something left over, I do not think it is proper that you should come to parliament and get authority to borrow money as capital to replace that $800,000. That is not the way business is done, and the harbour commission should not conduct its affairs on that principle if the object is to maintain low tolls. I am sure the minister desires to do everything possible to improve transportation facilities at Vancouver and I know he realizes the importance of the tolls question to the farmers of Alberta. Alberta is seriously affected in this matter and it is of the utmost consequence that, wherever possible, improvements should be effected out of surplus revenues. Surplus revenues mean that, as a result of larger business, more tolls have been charged than otherwise would be the case. The tolls are fixed on the basis of 32649-96
a smaller volume of business, and as the volume increases the tolls bring in a correspondingly larger revenue. When this revenue surplus accumulates-and my submission is that is was not contemplated that there should be this larger revenue by reason of an increased volume of business-the surplus might properly be made available for needed capital expenditures so as to prevent the possibility of borrowings, which of course involve interest charges which must be made up by an increase in tolls. I can see that the minister has given the matter his consideration. It is a question which is not wholly free from, shall I say, grave results to those who supply the commodities which pay the tolls whereby the interest obligations of the commission are discharged.

The people of Alberta are very much interested in the harbour of Vancouver. This year the Vancouver harbour commissioners appealed to the Board of Grain Commissioners to increase the tariff charges for handling grain through the elevator, and although the Alberta government protested, these increased charges, I believe, are now in effect. I do not know whether I understood the minister correctly, but that is what I thought he said. This state of affairs, I think, justifies the attitude of the people of Alberta and the action of the Alberta members during the past year in endeavouring to secure a representative of the grain producers from that province on the harbour board. I think we are supplying the tonnage which provides half the revenues of the port of Vancouver, and it does seem to me that the government might very well have given to the wheat producers of Alberta representation on the board. It is well known that there is a good deal of dissatisfaction in Alberta over the make-up of the Vancouver harbour board, and it is to be regretted that the government did not give some consideration to the claim of Alberta to have a representative of their own on the board. I hope that- the minister, when he introduces the bill, will be able to give complete information regarding not only the matters which have been referred to to-day, but also in relation to the purchase of the Hastings mill site and the development which the harbour commissioners contemplate at that point. I should like him to give information also regarding the cost of construction of No. 2 elevator. It is important for us to know whether the parties who are



Vancouver Harbour Commission
negotiating for tihe lease of elevator No. 1 are to be charged a rental based on the cost of construction of this elevator. There is no comparison in the cost of elevator No. 1 and the cost of elevator No. 2. No. 1 was constructed by the government, under whose ownership it was operated, and it was later turned over to the Vancouver harbour commission at a cost of $550,000, which was only a little over 50 per cent of what the elevator was worth. I desire to make a few
observations regarding this rather important matter. In the first place, I support what my hon. friend (Mr. Coote) has just said in reference to fees. When the elevator fees in connection with the Vancouver harbour were increased I publicly opposed it and I urged the commissioners not to apply for the advance. I felt that the fees at that time were sufficient to pay for the cost of administration and operation, and I have no hesitation now in supporting my hon. friend's view in that respect. Furthermore, when the tonnage fee was increased from one cent to six cents per ton I considered that also too large an increase.
As regards the proposal for a representative on the Vancouver harbour commission from the province of Alberta, I would suggest to the government the advisability of enlarging the commission by increasing its membership to five and slightly changing its constitution. At present there are three commissioners, the chairman receiving a salary of $6,000 and the other two commissioners $4,000 each. The minister will correct me if I am wrong. After a long experience covering a number of years in connection with the operation of the commission, I have come to the conclusion that it would be better to have a chairman paid a salary of six or eight thousand dollars, and four commissioners who should receive an honorarium of about $2,000. These figures are of course arbitrary: they are not at all definite, being only a suggestion. These junior commissioners, if I may so describe them, need not necessarily be expected to give all their time to the commission; that is to say, it should not be a job for them. Rather they could sit as directors, meeting once or twice a month and dealing with matters of general policy of the board. In that way you could secure the services of some very eminent authorities on the classes of business transacted, such as a prominent shipping man, a 
grain man thoroughly familiar with the internal handling of grain as well as the shipping of it, and a prominent businessman who would be willing to give his time in part to the study of harbour matters, advising and cooperating with the board on all questions of policy, without necessarily devoting himself to administration. At the present time- I speak from memory-the board has a general superintendent who receives about $8,000 a year. They have a superintendent of elevators, an assistant superintendent of elevators and a foreman of elevators, and I contend that these positions are in excess of their needs. It seems to me that one superintendent of elevators would be enough, and I doubt if either the assistant superintendent or the foreman is needed at all. The general superintendent of the whole harbour, with a foreman at each elevator, should be able properly to safeguard the interest of the commission, and in that way a considerable saving could be made.
With regard to the $1,500,000 mentioned by the minister, I think the correct explanation is that out of previous appropriations made by parliament there still remains about that sum. The commissioners have been carrying on very extensive works and have exceeded the authorized payment by this government; that is, the payments they make must be authorized by the -government, and while they have exceeded those payments by a considerable sum they have still kept within the general appropriation made by parliament. These extra moneys were paid, I understand, not all out of revenue, but partly in that way with the balance secured by an -overdraft at the bank. If I recall correctly statements I have seen, that overdraft amounted to about $600,000 and -this is a matter for which the commission might be criticized. I am not offering these remarks to the minister in a critical spirit at all, but rather that his hands may be strengthened in keeping proper control over this board as well as others. That overdraft of $600,000 was secured by the hypothecation of the securities represented by the sinking fund, which was an entirely wrong action on the part of the board. I think we must give the minister credit for having condemned this practice and for having corrected it, and I hope he will join with us in saying that it will not occur again.
It will not.

I think it is necessary foi the minister now to approve-and in the reorganization of the board I assume that he has considered and has approved of this over

Vancouver Harbour Commission
draft-expenditures which are covered by previous appropriations by parliament to the extent of approximately $1,500,000.

Might I ask a question, just for information? Would it be necessary for the minister to bring this matter of $1,500,000 before parliament? Would it not be only necessary for him to give his approval to it?

I commend the minister for having done so; he need not have brought it before parliament, and I think he deserves great credit for having been frank with us. He has made a complete statement, and I may say frankly that all he needed to do was to ask for a certain sum, namely $4,000,000, to be used for future purposes, and to show how it was to be expended. But there was this unexplained and unaccounted-for difference for which the harbour board should have been criticized; I have not the slightest doubt that the minister and the deputy minister have criticized them strongly and bitterly for it, but it is as well to discipline these boards occasionally to keep them within bounds.
Before I pass on I would like to refer to the Woodward elevator, which was the reason for this lease of the Oriental Grain Company. That property should never have been purchased from Woodward originally; I wrote a letter to the commissioners in the autumn of 1922 or 1923, before they asked the approval of the government at all, and warned them that it was an improvident action, that they would have nothing but trouble if they purchased it, and that so far as I was concerned I would keep my skirts clear of it. They went on with the negotiations, and came to Ottawa where they finally secured the approval of the government to the taking over of the Woodward elevator. This project was originally entered into by a gentleman named Woodward, a grain man from Winnipeg, in which business he was a failure; he got into trouble and obligated himself to buy a large piece of waterfront on which he built a cheap structure, aftijr which he went into a condition of bankruptcy. The harbour commissioners took over his whole bag of tricks and troubles, which never should have been done; following that there was an expenditure of public money to put the elevator into proper shape, which work was estimated to cost $600,000, but really required $1,000,000. The elevator now is probably in good condition; I do not question that, but the whole trouble from start to finish, including that connected with this Oriental Grain Company, came in the train of this original action, and I know that the harbour commissioners and the government have spent a good many 32649-96^
anxious days wondering just how to extricate themselves from the results of that improvident action. 1 am not going to say that the government should not make a settlement; that is something no one should declare without having very carefully examined all the papers, but I do say that in making a settlement the government should scrutinize with great care any claim based upon that original transaction.

He still tt'ould have the power to impose both fine and imprisonment. We are merely leaving it to the discretion of the judge as to whether both fine and imprisonment shall be imposed.
That was the whole bone of contention in the discussion of last year.

If I were sure that it would have the effect that my hon. friend fears I would not suggest making any change, because, as I say, I want to make it certain that the smuggler will be punished. But I do not want to go so far as to make it obligatory upon the court to imprison a man who, after all, has no intention of smuggling, and I say that it is quite conceivable that that might be the case; he might remove the goods, for instance, before examination or payment of duty. He might be ignorant of the law. Many people do not know the law so well as perhaps hon. members of this House, and if an innocent person did that, the judge would have no option; he would have to send him to gaol. I would not like that to happen. If the judge in his wisdom 
decides that the man did it with the intention of smuggling, he has the power to impose not only the fine but imprisonment as well. It seems to me that perhaps the other might be just a little bit too drastic.
I am sorry, but I must conclude with protesting against the minister making the change. I warn him now that he is making a serious mistake.

Coming from the prairies as I do, from a part of the country box-dering on the Dakota boundary, I can fully appreciate what the minister has said. In my opinion this section is a little drastic as applied to a sparsely settled country such as we have on the prairies. We have a number of farmers in the constituency I represent, and the same thing applies all along the border of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, whose closest point to market is in the state of Dakota or Montana, as the case may be. They will probably go over to the nearest town on the other side of the border and buy a line of machinery with the intention of paying the duty, but on the way home they find there is not a custom house to which they can report within probably twelve or fifteen miles, and consequently they go home with their line of machinery intending to report at the nearest custom house at the first opportunity, but that may not be for several days sometimes. Now if this section passes, that man will be considered a criminal for those days in which he has failed to report. This section may be all right for the purpose intended. I am not trying to defend the professional smuggler by any means, but I am concerned about the man on the land who intends to carry on his business legitimately, but who owing to the long distance from the custom house does not find it convenient to report immediately.
I think also that there should be an easy method of appeal from the decision of these two justices of the peace who are mentioned in this section. I do not think that too much should depend on the judgment of two justices of the peace in imprisonment cases. I think there should be an easy method of appeal from their decision. To sum up, I think this legislation is entirely too drastic for a sparsely settled country such as our prairies.	i

No, but it is quite possible to make the punishment altogether out of proportion to the crime. There was a time in the old country when under the law a man could be hanged for stealing sheep, but no one was hanged because they could not get a conviction. It is not necessary for the judge to impose seven years. He can use discretion.

I think the whole section is vicious. My hon. friend speaks about putting a premium on smuggling. He raised a great disturbance last year on the question of smuggling. It seems to me he went after the crudest form of smuggling- the man who smuggles something over the border, gets caught and has to go to gaol for seven years. But the man who smuggles a word into the customs tariff can get all the goods into the country he likes, free of duty, and goes off scot-free. There is a section in the customs tariff which says that wool of a kind and class produced in Canada shall bear three cents a pound duty. There is another section which says that the wool and the hair of the camel, alpaca, and so on shall come in free. We find that the friends of my hon. friend who are so concerned 'about putting a stop to smuggling can get all their raw wool in free by smuggling the word "wool" into another part of the tariff. Those are the people who are defrauding the country of revenue. If you take a man who smuggles an article into this country, or who is found in this country with the article in his possession, and send him to gaol for seven years, you bring the whole tariff into disrepute among the people, and it will bring the government into disrepute among the people. If you try to enforce such a provision as that you will find that the whole customs law will stink in the nostrils of right thinking people. I protest against it.

I do not suppose I can prevent the section from carrying, but I would like to enter a word of protest against subsection (a). It is altogether too severe. If a man smuggles in a shirt I suppose he would be liable to a fine of $50 and imprisonment for a year. I would like to see a section inserted in our Customs Act similar to that in force in the United States, which country is always held up to us as an example of the high tariff. The citizens of the United States may once a year bring in goods up to the value, I think, of $100, without paying duty, simply by making a declaration that they have not previously in that year taken any goods into that country. Everyone who goes from this country across the line would probably like to bring in some little article when he returns, and under this act if he did not declare it he is liable to this fine of $50 and possibly imprisonment.

For a number of years I was in the customs administering one of the chief ports of New Brunswick, and during eight years of that time I was engaged in detecting smuggling on the high seas and on the border. secuting. If I mistake not, to-day the regulation is that where the seizure does not exceed two hundred dollars in value the officer is to report to the department for instructions. I live in a province that is almost surrounded by the sea and on the land side we are bounded by the state of Maine and the province of Quebec. Where the customs officials had to close their offices to attend to some other important business, and the returning Canadian had no opportunity to declare any purchases that he had made during his visit, I have known officious officials to institute proceedings for violation of the law. I think with the section in its present form our friends may rest assured that very little injustice will be done to those who may be trapped in that way,

I would like to support the views of the hon. member for Quebec South. I look upon a gaol sentence as being very severe, probably not so much on the man who is sentenced, but upon his wife and children. It is something that will follow them to the grave.

We have enough crimes now in our criminal code without taking up the time of parliament in making more.
There is this further consideration. In the reorganization of the Customs department, I understand that there is to be at the head of the preventive service a man who hitherto has been dealing with the underworld, a man who has been in charge of the narcotic squad, in charge of the police whose duty it is to prevent the smuggling of goods into this country. This man must of necessity be someone who will not have the discretion and tact and the feeling necessary to deal with ordinary cases of non-commercial smuggling.
Customs Act Amendment

I doubt very much whether it is wise on our part to put at the head of the preventive service a man of that calibre. I am not saying anything derogatory of his character, for he must have been a man of some strength of character and of will to deal with the people with whom he had to deal. But when cases come before him such as he will have to deal with under this act he will be entirely out of his element, and I for one object to his being given the power which I suppose he will be given under this act to prosecute for violations of the law.
I would suggest to the minister that the term of imprisonment be not less than six months and not more than two years. Why, you can commit almost any crime on the calendar and get away with seven years, and I do not see why a specially made crime, as the result of agitation during the course of the last year or so, should be punishable to such a degree as it is under this act.

I do not see why in paragraph (b) the same option is not given as in paragraph (a). If the value of the goods is under $200, then the person convicted is liable on conviction to a fine or to imprisonment, or both; that is paragraph (a).
An amendment has been proposed.

I was not aware of that. In regard to what has been said as to the penalty being too severe, perhaps it is. At the same time, with whom are you dealing? If a man has courage enough to break into a bank or hold you up on the highway-and he is taking chances in doing that-and he gets away with a few thousand dollars, you would not say that seven years was too much for him; not at all, serves him right; and yet he had the quality of courage at all events. But here you are dealing with wholesale thieves, with men who are stealing not in small quantities but making q business of stealing wholesale.
Not altogether.

To a large extent. I am referring now to the class of smuggler referred to by the minister himself, the man who has to be dealt with severely because be is making a practice of smuggling, as they have been doing in this country, stealing from the public revenues, not thousands, but millions and millions of dollars. I have no sympathy to waste on these people at all, not a bit. In so far as this is general and applies to all convictions for smuggling, I want to say that in my estimation it is not severe enough.

In dealing with these people who are engaged in the smuggling of narcotics, you should not stop at seven years; you should put them in prison for life. Better still, to save the country expense, they ought to be taken out and hanged. That is the way to deal with these people. There is no joke about that at all, because the men who are engaged for gain in the smuggling of narcotics are committing murder by degrees-the worst kind of murder. I have less regard for them than I have for the man who in a fit of passion kills his fellow-man ; and I would deal with them just as severely as it was possible to deal with them. It may be that the term of imprisonment might be modified to some extent, but as to those who are going to make a business of smuggling, a business of wholesale stealing from the revenues of the country, men who are thieves and nothing but thieves, the law is there, and they disregard the law for the purpose of personal gain. I do not see, therefore, that they are entitled to any sympathy at all. I want to add a word of commendation of the minister for, the vigorous manner in which he has undertaken to deal with these people. He deserves all kind of credit, and I wish him every success in his task.

Since the session was opened it has been made clearly manifest that we are going to maintain a customs tariff. This House has declared so by two votes, and if we are going to maintain a customs, tariff, surely we must have some penalties for violation of the act. I agree in a large measure with what the Minister of Customs has proposed, that the penalty should be severe. However, I am entirely in accord with the suggestion made by the Postmaster General of allowing goods to the value of $50 to be brought into this country free by tourists. The Customs Tariff Act of the United States provides in paragraph 1695 that:
Clothing actually owned by persons and in their possession at the time of their departure from a foreign country-
Shall be admitted, and paragraph 1696 provides that:
Articles acquired abroad by residents of the United States for personal or household use, or as souvenirs or curios, but not bought on commission or intended for sale, up to, but not exceeding a total of one hundred dollars.
Shall be admitted free. I think if a good stiff penalty is imposed for actual smuggling, and some such regulation as they have in the United States Tariff Act is included in ours with regard to tourists bringing in a small quantity of goods, the difficulty that has been suggested here to-night will largely be overcome. The ruling given by the United

Customs Act Amendment
States customs officials in the port of Detroit is that these goods shall be admitted free when brought in by bona-fide tourists touring abroad. It does seem to me that when we are going to have a customs tariff-and it seems we are, and a good high one, much to my regret-we have to have a stiff penalty for infractions of the law, but I believe that tourists should be allowed to bring goods up to the value of $50 or $100' into Canada, just as the American tourists are allowed to take goods back when returning to their country.

I am quite sure that all
members of the House are willing to support the minister in anything that will effectually deal with the professional smuggler. I wonder if instead of changing the word "and" to "or" in the third line of paragraph (b) he would make it read:
In the case of a previous conviction.
So that if the smuggler has been previously convicted the magistrate would have no option, but to commit him to gaol.

We have a section later on
in the bill dealing with the same offence.
I was not aware of that, but would not this be a good place to put it?

This section seems to have
caused a great deal of discussion because of the penalty features of it. There are several other sections that also deal with penalty. I have no desire to force the measure through even if I could. I am quite willing to give it consideration. Possibly we might go on with certain sections which do not include this feature.

Will the hon. minister consider an amendment to item 690A in the regulations? There has been talk of considerable latitude being allowed to tourists who bring in personal belongings. I wish to refer to the conditions that exist in some isolated communities. On the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway in the West Kootenay district the port of entry is Revelstoke. Many of the residents in the district along the Arrow lakes for a distance of one hundred miles are largely English families and at Christmas time they receive their plum pudding and other Christmas remembrances, but with great regularity those settlers are put to considerable inconvenience. They claim that these Christmas gifts should be admitted under the casual donations provision. I have in mind two concrete cases. For instance, at Christmas time a family in that district received from their own relatives in England a Christmas
pudding and it was necesary to conduct a lot of correspondence with those families because they cannot get up to Revelstoke and back in less than three days to present their claim. The consequence was that last Christmas one family in that district did not receive their Christmas gifts. In the case of a haggis the customs collector went so far as to charge fifty-two cents to the family receiving it. Last Christmas season some of the families along the Arrow lakes did not receive their -Christmas gifts from the old country until a week after the Christmas festival. Their plum puddings were held up-
Oh, oh!

It may be a joke to some
hon. members, but it is no joke to these people. They are isolated and living about a hundred miles from the customs house and they are put to serious inconvenience until letters are sent back and forth between the customs officials and these people. In another case a charge of forty-two cents was collected from a settler for some shortbread sent from the old country for a Christmas present. Surely the customs officials should be permitted to exercise some little discretionary power in reference to Christmas presents. People expect to pay duty when they are sending to the old country to purchase goods, but when the parcels are marked "Christmas presents" I think the minister should ask the customs officer at Revelstoke to exercise a little common sense and let the parcels come in duty free.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister suggests that sections 15 to 20, both inclusive, stand.

I think there has been some little confusion between the granting of the authority to impose a penalty and the imposition of the maximum penalty. It does not follow that because the power is there it has to be exercised. Some of the observations that have been made would lead one to believe that hon. members were fearful that judges would, for a first offence, impose imprisonment of seven years in addition to the fine. We all know that that is out of the question. I quite agree with the section as drawn by the minister and presented to the House, and I believe it should be passed.

I would like to remind the hon. member for West Calgary of a little quotation with which he is quite familiar:
How oft the sight of means to do ill deeds
Makes ill deeds done!
Customs Act Amendment

I am so delighted that the hon. member has made that observation, because it shows how little he understands the character of the legislation. This is a judicial power, and it is subject to correction by the court to stop ill deeds, and ant to make them done. Furthermore, it is a judicial power, and if anything wrong is done by the magistrate under our jurisprudence it is always open to the person who may be aggrieved to avail himself of the remedy accorded to him.
The poor man who cannot pay the fine must go to gaol; he cannot go to a higher court, by way of appeal.

I am sure the solicitude of the hon. gentleman for those whom we heard of last winter will be received in some quarters as an act of very great grace indeed, and as indicating a sympathy for that class of the community that is much required.
Sections 15 to 20 stand.
Sections 21, 22 and 23 agreed' to.
Look at section
We are past that section.

It should not have passed. The same principle is involved here. Consider the penalty there-imposing on the man for having goods on the boundary line a fine not exceeding 11,000, or not less than $200, and to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not less than one month, or to both fine and imprisonment. I object to that section. It is in the same class with section 15.
It has been carried.
Not carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declared the clause carried. If the committee wish it may be reconsidered.
It may stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On the suggestion of the minister clause 23 stands.
If clauses are to be slipped by in this way and if when an hon. member asks that a clause be reconsidered it cannot be reconsidered, we must protect ourselves by insisting that every clause be read.

I have suggested that it
stand.

Thank you.
Section 24 agreed to.
On section 25-Being on board of smuggling vessel-penalty.
Here is another imprisonment penalty. I suggest that this clause also stand over.

How would
it be to take all the penalties out of every infraction of the law? That is apparently what the hon. gentleman wants.

The hon. gentleman seems to think that any man found in the company of a smuggler or with smuggled goods in his possession is a thief and a coward. If I understand the law aright, a man found with stolen goods in his possession loses the goods; but we are providing here that if he is found with smuggled goods in his possession he is to be treated worse than a thief.

He is worse
than a thief.
That is a nice sense of morality.

Let me cite
the case of a young fellow as honest and honourable as any man born in Nova Scotia-
Oh, oh.
He came from Lunenburg, I suppose.

If any man has anything to say against Nova Scotia let him
say it.
You have just said it.
I am going to cite the case of a young man as honest and honourable as any man born in Nova Scotia.
Oh, oh.

I say a young man perfectly honest. He happened to be on a boat off that coast, a boat that he understood was engaged in legitimate trade. Outside the three mile limit at the point of a gun he was compelled to do something that he found very odious indeed. Under this section that man would be branded a criminal.
No.

We must be
careful in this legislation. I say again, there is no class of criminal that I detest more than

Customs Act Amendment
the smuggler. Last year the customs scandal occupied most of our time and attention, with the result that these amendme)nts are so drastic that they may bring the whole law into disrepute. Surely we have had sufficient experience to know that when we make penalties too severe we defeat the object we have in view and weaken rather than strengthen the law. With respect to the insinuation of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), I recall two cases of a similar nature, disagreeable cases, it is true, and one judge imposed a sentence of ten years and the other a sentence of six months. I have the highest regard for our judiciary, but when we hear of these marked variations in the penalties imposed for the same offence, we must be very careful that we ourselves are not responsible for enacting laws of such a drastic nature that they bring the whole law into contempt.

I notice that in the
third line of 216 .the term "one league" is used. I presume the minister means three miles. This term is subject to misunderstanding, and as the words "three miles" are used almost everywhere throughout the act I suggest that this section be amended accordingly.
I have no objection at all.

I move, Mr. Chairman,
that the words "one league" in the third line of 216 be changed to read "three miles."
Three statute miles.

We had better be careful
to distinguish between statute miles and marine miles.

A statute mile is shorter
than a marine mile, but I am not particular. The term "league" is out of date altogether.

I think we should make
it read "three marine miles."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Clause 25 stands.
On Section 26-Keeping or selling, etc., goods unlawfully imported-forfeiture-burden of proof.

I think the opening lines:
If any person, whether the owner or not, without lawful excuse, the proof of which shall be on the person accused,

-are most objectionable. I do not know of any criminal act in which the accused is presumed to be guilty. A man charged with the most brutal murder is entitled to a fair trial, and the crown must adduce such evidence as will convince the jury that the
accused is guilty. In this case a man who is on board a vessel which is liable to suspicion may be condemned-I suppose the conviction again is gaol1 for seven years-unless he can clearly show to two justices of the peace- who more often than not are uneducated and likely to be prejudiced-that he is not engaged in smuggling. As I have already stated, I think we are going altogether too far in these amendments. We are violating the very elementary rights of British subjects. I am surprised that my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), who is one of the most staunch defenders of the rights of his fellow citizens, does not rise in his wrath and verbally smite the minister for daring to impose such penalties as are prescribed in this section. The very roots of individual liberty are being attacked, and I would suggest that the minister give careful consideration to this proposal before it passes into law.

This proposal is copied
closely from the Customs Act in connection with an offence which it seems to me is milder than the one now under consideration. In that case it is provided that anyone who without lawful excuse, proof of which he himself shall establish, sends or brings into Canada or, being in this country, has in his possession any bill-heading or other paper or blank to be filled up and used as an invoice, shall be guilty of an indictable offence. That offence is not nearly so grave as the one under review.

That paper is used for
purposes of fraud.
Yes.

Will the minister mention
an instance of lawful excuse?

I am not a legal man and
I cannot interpret the law.
I am grateful to my hon friend (Mr. Power) for his observations as to my desire always to voice sentiments that favour the liberty of the subject. That however is not what we are discussing.
It is.

The hon. member has
such a wide knowledge of everything that he reminds me of what was once said of Macaulay: "If I knew as much about anything as he pretends to know about everything I should indeed be wise". I hesitate to make the remark I am about to make. Is there a desire on the part of the House to render nugatory all the efforts the minister has made to put on the statute book an
Customs Act Amendment

effective law to prevent a recurrence of the conditions we had disclosed last year? Is that the object? If not, why make a joke of all this, as some hon. gentlemen seem to be doing? The truth is that in all jurisprudence, as my hon. friend from Quebec South so well knows, there are certain conditions which in themselves are regarded as prima facie evidence either of negligence or of guilt. For example, according to law of negligence, if a person traveling on a passenger train is injured, the very .fact that the conveyance is one intended for passengers is prima facie evidence of negligence on the part of the company. We use the expression in law, res ipsa loquitur-the thing speaks for itself. So that in criminal cases where we have certain conditions which in themselves constitute an evidence of guilt, and therefore is prima facie proof of it, any person found in certain relationship to those conditions is presumed to be guilty of the offence involved. The onus of proving his innocence rests upon the person so found. In the particular section to which attention is called it will be observed that:
If any person. . . . harbours, keeps, conceals, purchases, sells or exchanges any goods unlawfully imported into Canada-
-he must prove a lawful excuse. That is all. Take our laws relating to liquors. As my hon. friend from Quebec South knows, in Quebec, in Alberta and in Saskatchewan, under certain conditions, the onus of proving innocence rests upon the accused. Once a person is found in certain circumstances the onus is shifted and he must explain his position. This happens every day in respect of many matters I need not mention.
I shall not speak to-night on this question, but I desire to say this much before I conclude. I followed with a good deal of interest and some degree of effort all that was said last year with respect to the enforcement of the customs laws, and I learned then that men were perfectly willing to pay $1,000 at any time if they could get away with $5,000. They were quite prepared to pay $1,000 now and $1,000 again if by so doing they could gain $10,000, and this effort on the part of the minister and the government, by making the penalty so severe as to prevent a recurrence of what has so marked the administration of the customs laws of the country, must commend itself to hon. members. 1 do not say that severe penalties will cure evils of this kind, because they do not. But where you have a condition prevailing, a known condition such as that disclosed last year, and you find men flourishing as they do by gains ill-gotten from smuggling and 
from the importation of narcotics, it is time we made the penalties severe enough. Drastic penalties in such cases are found to operate as a powerful preventive. Let me give an illustration; take the case of whipping. Hon. gentlemen will recall that a certain Cl ass of criminal was perfectly content to suffer imprisonment for burglary, for housebreaking, for bank robbery and offences of that nature; but the moment you added the cat-'o-nine tails he became less eager to carry on his operations. The reason is psychological, as those will understand who have studied criminology. I remember reading some time ago an eminent criminologist's opinion in this regard. There is something in the psychology of this form of punishment so repulsive to the mentality of the burglar that he will not readily risk the possible infliction of the penalty, which therefore proves a strong deterrent. Here you have a type of man engaged in smuggling on a large scale; he is a professional, a member of an organized gang or clique which is trying not only to defraud the country of its revenues, but, as the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington has said, to work irreparable physical injury on our citizens. He traffics in narcotics and other drugs. I am not talking about the casual smuggler who brings across a bolt of silk; I am concerned with the class who are known to engage in a business which is a menace to the lives of people, as brought out before the royal commission now7 carrying on its investigations.
So that no one would risk the penalty, would the hon. gentleman be prepared to suggest the death sentence in this case?

Nothing could better accentuate the observations I made when I rose to my feet than the interruption of my hon. friend. There are under our criminal law three offences which may be punished by death; treason, murder and rape. The other day a judge imposed the penalty of death upon an accused convicted in Ontario of the last named offence and the Court of Criminal Appeal set aside that sentence. The point I make is this. The discretion as to what the penalty and the punishment shall be must always rest with the judiciary, but we have surrounded it with rights of appeal under which I venture to say there have been in this country very few instances of grave wrong done to any individual by reason of the severity of the punishment imposed. In addition to that there is the executive power which may always be set in motion for the purpose of relieving a convicted person from a penalty if

Customs Act Amendment
under the circumstances there is evidence to warrant such action.
I am not going to trespass further on the time of the committee. I do say to my fellow members of this House, some of whom were not here last year, that if they have read the evidence given before that committee last year, and if they have been following the evidence given before the royal commission, they must realize the extent and the enormity of the injury being done to Canada through the loss of revenue. Not only have we been injured in that way, but also through the idea which has been going abroad in this country that by violating the law men may create great fortunes for themselves, and by their ostentatious display of their ilbgotten gains create feelings of envy and dissatisfaction in the minds of the decent people of this country. I think hon. members will agree that the time has come when we should at once say, "You are beyond the pale of our civilization, and the resources of that civilization are not yet exhausted against its enemies," to quote the language of Mr. Gladstone. We are now dealing with one of the resources of civilization, which civilization is threatened by the perils and evils which I have indicated without going into detail.
I suppose it is not usual for one on this side of the House to support an opposing minister with such warmth, but I know from what I have read and from what I have seen that we are facing great danger from the continuance of this condition in Canada, and it has become imperative that this gang of swindlers and smugglers can no longer become the leading men in their communities, displaying their ill-gotten gains, their high powered cars, their beautiful residences, their silks, satins and jewels, and thus arousing the envy of the less fortunate but honest people. We should brand them as criminals not only with a fine, but we should send them to the gaols of the country, and then and not till then will the laws of this country be observed.

I am quite willing to believe in the good faith of those hon. gentlemen who have made objections to this bill, and who plead that undue penalties will be imposed upon people who are morally innocent. At the same time, I am inclined to fear that if the demands for the emasculation of this bill are successful it will leave the department with nothing more than a popgun with which to fight this evil. I think the knowledge gained last year through the sittings of that committee brought to our notice a condition of things which we must face in a most determined manner. Personally I am disposed to agree very heartily with the provisions which have been incorporated in the bill; some small amendments may be necessary, but in the main I believe we must adopt desperate remedies to cure desperate diseases. It may be true that ignorant and illiterate justices of the peace, men not accustomed to dealing with the law, may occasionally visit undue punishment upon individuals, but at the same time we must take that into account in all our laws, and we cannot depart from a sound principle because exceptional cases of hardship may arise. We must expect that that will be the case, but we cannot make laws to deal with exceptional cases. I repeat, I am afraid that if the suggestions of many hon. members are carried too far we will have nothing left which will be effective in meeting the condition of affairs which confronts us. I know in dealing with this question with the electors last fall I emphasized the need of considerable drastic measures to meet the deplorable condition revealed by the customs inquiry last year.

I would quite agree with
the last two speakers if the majority of the people of Canada were professional smugglers, but those who carry on smuggling on a commercial scale are in the minority. If the resources of civilization are not exhausted, as my hon. friend has well said, surely we can find some means to punish these commercial smugglers without treating the whole population of our country as smugglers.
They will not be affected at all.

I will go further. My friend says the resources of civilization are not exhausted. Why, then, does he go back to the days of barbarism to find heavy punishments to inflict upon the people of this country? Many years ago sheep stealing was punishable by hanging; did that prevent sheep stealing? I think not; I am quite sure that on the contrary it prevented hanging. We are imposing heavy penalties on the people of Canada for infractions of the tariff law, while a large portion of the people of this country and a fair proportion of the members of this House regard any tariff law as morally wrong. So you place them in the dilemma of either following the dictates of their own conscience or violating the laws of the land. I do not agree with many who, like the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) may feel that the imposition of a tariff is morally wrong, but I do think consideration should be given to their views and that the penalties for carrying out what is after all no moral wrong to them should not be so heavy.
Customs Act Amendment

Perhaps my hon. friend
would ask the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) whether the restrictions on the sale of liquor are morally wrong.

I am not at all interested
in the views of the hon. member for Rose-town in regard to the restriction of the sale of liquor. I can quite sympathize with him if he feels that to a certain extent they are too drastic, but I do not wish to be brought into a controversy on that matter. I simply wish to point out to the minister that while for the time being he may have the sympathy of a majority in this House and perhaps of the majority of the people, he will find endless trouble in carrying out this act; time and again there will be brought to his attention cases of unfortunate people who have been unjustly condemned, and within a short time, in order to be workable, the act will have to be made far more lenient.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? He stated1 this section was interfering -with the liberty of the people; I do not agree with him, but the word's are his. Does he not think that this is a case of sin following sin, of precedent piled upon precedent, since we made the fatal error the ether day of interfering with free speech in this House?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman is right.

I would like to go back to the question I asked a few minutes ago, to which I would like an answer. I know that some time ago some gentlemen from Montreal went to the fprovinee of Nova Scotia and sold several automobiles that had been smuggled into Canada although they produced prima face evidence that the duty had been paid. I believe the victims are getting back their cars upon payment of the duty, and I see that the section as it stood previously was as follows:
If any person knowingly harbours, keeps, conceals purchases, sells or exchanges any goods unlawfully imported into Canada, whether such goods are dutiable or not, or whereon the duties lawfully payable have not been paid, such goods, if found, shall be seized and forfeited without power of remission, and, if such goods are not found, the person so offending shall forfeit the value thereof without power of remission.
That would appear to me as quite reasonable and proper, but I can quite understand that it may have been difficult in a great many instances to prove guilty knowledge on persons who had such goods in their possession. What I would1 like to know.now is whether the proposed section makes any

change in the law other than shifting the burden of proof. The new clause reads:
If any person, whether the owner or not, without lawful excuse. . . . harbours, keeps conceals, purchases-
And so on. Does that moan:
If any person, without knowing the goods to have been smuggled, harbours, keeps, conceals, purchases.
It is important that we know this. How can a person in whose possession are found smuggled goods, escape the penalty? How can he go into court and show that he has a lawful excuse? Supposing he says that he was furnished with some sort of entry paper, would it be said by the court that he should have looked into and satisfied himself as to the genuineness of it? Would that be a sufficient answer by the crown to the excuse which he was offering? That is an, important matter in that connection. I understand this is a copy of another section, and it may be that it is ample protection to the person who is accused, but the uncertainty should be cleared up. With regard to the general question of penalties, it is very important that we should scrutinize them, because undoubtedly the imposition of penalties which are too severe will not serve the object of carrying out the act properly.
Mr. EULE'R:	I regret very much that I
could not hear all my hon. friend was saying. If I heard him correctly, what I did hear was that he was objecting to the fact that formerly the clause contained the word "knowingly," and that word is now 'being replaced by the words "without lawful excuse." If that is his objection, the answer to that is simply this: It is practically impossible in these cases to prove that a man knew and so to secure a conviction. Under this clause he is given the privilege of making a lawful excuse. Just what form that may take, I am not able to say. It may be given in various ways.
Mr. ILSLEY': Does the minister not think it is important to know that? There are men all over the country who may be proceeded against.

There is no doubt whatever that people were found unlawfully and knowingly in possession of smuggled goods, but it was impossible to show that they were knowingly in possession of those goods. We are now making it a little more difficult for those people to escape.

In other words, I understand the object of the minister is to have the opportunity of reaching all the guilty

Customs Act Amendment
parties, but with no opportunity for innocent parties, if they cannot prove their innocence, to escape. This is enlarging a very dangerous principle. I have always understood that from the point of view of moral law, as well as practical legislation, we should rather run the risk of letting one guilty party escape than of unduly punishing an innocent party. That is the great danger of legislation of this nature. I quite realize the object of the minister. Undoubtedly there is great difficulty in coping with the evil that was brought to the attention of the House last session by the committee of inquiry, but at the same time we should not let ourselves be impressed too much by the findings of that committee and we should think more of the dangers which we may run by introducing legislation that will either be impossible of application or work undue injury to people who will not be in a position to prove their innocence and thus to escape the penalties as they are provided for in this legislation.
Everybody knows that amongst officials of any department and especially those which are charged with the imposition of penalties, there exists the practice of enabling officers of the law to partake of the advantages of pursuit. Therefore they develop the spirit of finding guilty parties even when they do not exist and of endeavouring by all means to have parties found guilty in regard to whose guilt there is a doubt. They do this in order to justify their activities, to further their advancement with their chief, and to bring revenue to themselves. This is fully as great a danger to public morality as the amount of smuggling that may be done more or less under the application of a milder law.
If we had such a principle of severe punishment and such principles of evidence in all our criminal law with regard to offences of a much more immoral nature than those which are provided for by this legislation, the policy would be a general one; but as the matter stands now, with the leniency that is shown to such a variety and quantity of criminals and swindlers, especially in the financial world, I do not think the conscience of the country will be prepared to sustain a law of tliis nature and to make it easy for the government to carry it out. I think with the various members who have expressed the same opinion that the minister had better consider this matter further before it is passed definitely.

Section agreed to.
Section 27 agreed to.
On section 28-Smuggling carrying offensive weapons.

I object to this clause which reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offense and liable to imprisonment for ten years, who while carrying offensive weapons is found with any goods liable to seizure or forfeiture under this act or any law relating to the customs, knowing such goods to be so liable.
Any hon. member knows very well that a large number of people who travel carry revolvers.
No.

I know they do. Perhaps they do not need to do so in Nova Scotia where my vociferous friends come from; but a great number of people, when they are travelling abroad, let us say, carry revolvers. It is known to a considerable number of hon. members that people think very little of bringing in a few packages of cigarettes or, if they are ladies, of bringing in two or three pairs of silk stockings. If you have that combination, an offensive weapon, such as a small revolver, and a pair of silk stockings found in the handbag of a lady coming across the border, she is liable to ten years' imprisonment. I simply point that out to the committee.
I might say that this clause is copied bodily from the criminal code. There is nothing new in it at all.

Section agreed to.
On section 29-Vessel leaving without a clearance, etc.

This deals with the case of a vessel departing from a port in Canada without a clearance, and other very serious crimes, but the master of the vessel incurs a penalty of only $400, unless the cargo comprises wines or spirituous liquors, when the penalty is $1,000. There is no talk of imprisonment in this case, I notice. It says:
If any vessel departs from any port or place in Canada without a clearance, or if the master delivers a false content, or does not truly answer the questions demanded of him-[DOT]
-only a small fine of $400 is imposed, but the chap caught with smuggled goods in his possession, possibly not for commercial use at all, is liable to a penalty of seven years imprisonment. The two things do not go well together.

Surely the hon. gentleman must know that a vessel departing from a port in Canada without a clearance is entirely
Customs Act Amendment

different from smuggling goods into the country. This is merely the case of a vessel departing without a clearance. It is not a very grave offence as compared with smuggling goods into the country.

In the opinion of many who took part in the customs investigation last year, and in the opinion of many thousands in the country, the trouble in Canada in the last few years has arisen from the desire to make money illegally through smuggling goods out of the country, and incidentally smuggling other goods in on the return journey. I say that if it is wrong to do one thing it is wrong to do the other. It is certainly wrong to allow a vessel to smuggle goods out of the country.' We should not allow this contrast to stand. A vessel engaged in illegal smuggling operations escapes with a fine of $400, -but the poor individual caught with a few smuggled goods in his possession is liable -to a long term of imprisonment. I do not think the Canadian people will approve of legislation of that kind or will be morally behind it.
It has stood for fifty years.
That does not make it any better.

I think the penalty
should be increased.

I want to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Melfort. It seems to me that these sections are in very, very great contrast. In one there is a very heavy fine and seven years' imprisonment imposed for a comparatively trivial offence, but in this case, where the social effects are very much more serious, there is imposed only a comparatively small fine, a fine that does not amount to anything in comparison with the value of the goods involved. If the hon. member for West Calgary found it necessary a little while ago to call upon this House to protect the country against vice, I do not see why he is silent at this time, because it seems to me we have essentially an evil here. I cannot see the distinction the minister is making between smuggling goods out of the country and smuggling goods into the country. If the minister was simply thinking in terms of a few little merchants who may be affected I could understand it but I do not think that is his calibre, and I would ask him to distinguish very clearly between these two classes of crime, the one smuggling goods out of the country, and the other smuggling goods in. I do not understand the distinction he draws.

The fact that a vessel leaves a port without obtaining a clearance is not proof at all that she is smuggling goods out of the country. You cannot smuggle goods out of a country, so far as that is concerned. The mere fact that a vessel is leaving without a clearance may be an offence, but it is no proof of smuggling goods into any country, whereas when goods come into a country illegally, that is smuggling. There is a distinction; in the one case there is smuggling; in the other -there is not necessarily smuggling.

That is quite true, but some of us who have followed the revelations of what has been happening on the western coast, which have been given considerable publicity in all our papers, and especially those of us who are resident in the west and have some knowledge of what has been going on, know that vessels have deliberately left ports ostensibly for Mexico or some other distant point, and the next day have arrived back in port again for another cargo. That seems to be fairly good evidence that there is something very wrong in such a procedure. What is the good of punishing the little man,, putting him in gaol because he may have smuggled a few dollars worth of goods into the country, and allowing the man who is making a fortune to go scot free? I do not think the minister has at all answered my question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the committee to adopt the section?
I think, Mr. Chairman, we have the right to hear from the minister a better explanation than he has so far offered.

I regret very much that the
hon. gentleman does not comprehend what I say.

It may be due to
my ignorance, but I listened to the minister and I cannot see that he has given a reason that will warrant us in passing a clause of this character. I think in view of the serious character of the smuggling that has gone on on the Pacific coast, we should have some further explanation of this clause.

If it is the wish of the
committee I have no objection to making the penalty greater; not at all; it is merely a matter of degree. But I do not think that the fact of a vessel leaving port without obtaining clearance is nearly so great an offence as smuggling goods into the country.

Customs Act Amendment

Would my hon. friend
permit me? Perhaps I can assist a little in this matter. There are two things involved; there is the clearance of the vessel, and then there is the violation, if any, of the law in regard to the cargo of the vessel. Both these things are dealt with in this act. One of them simply involves the obtaining of a clearance by the captain; the other is where the cargo is composed of liquor, and that is what this whole thing refers to. There is a bond put up by the owners of the liquor, who may not be the owners of the vessel at all. That bond is for double the value of the goods, and in order to secure the release of that bond the owners of the liquor must produce a landing certificate. The whole trouble on the Pacific coast, as well as on the Atlantic coast, as was disclosed both by the committee of last year and by the royal commission was that the owners of this liquor were suspected of giving false landing certificates, and in some cases that was fully demonstrated. That is the crime to which my hon. friend refers. That is the offence which ought to be penalized very heavily, and I understand that we have already passed a clause-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-which deals with that very question of the landing certificate.
What is the penalty?
I cannot say from memory. I think the privilege which had been granted by Canada is now practically wiped out.

That is the in transitu
shipment of liquor.

Yes, it is now practically
done away with. It grew up out of that practice. But the clearance of the vessel is a different thing altogether. Here is what really inspired-shall I say?-this amendment, particularly on the Atlantic coast; because on the Pacific coast it was carried on in a different way, on a larger scale altogether with larger boats. On the Atlantic coast there are smaller boats, fishing vessels and boats of that type that used to slip out of port without getting a proper clearance, and would then run to Rum Row or some other part of the coast. It is to deal with them that the penalty of $1,000 has been put in, in addition to the penalty of $400 which has been in the act for a long time. That fine is imposed on the owner of the vessel, the captain usually in the case of small vessels.
Another case in point was those vessels plying between St. Pierre-Miquelon, and Halifax. It was found that occasionally
liquor would be smuggled, not by the vessel or the owners of it, but by parties engaging space in the vessel. This penalty is against the master or owner of the vessel for violating the law, so far as the clearance side of it is concerned. In addition to that there is the violation of the bonding privilege which carries with it an altogether separate penalty.
I am not arguing the sufficiency of this. I am quite willing to support an increase of the penalty, but I am pointing out that there are two things involved, not merely one.

I recognize that
there are two things involved, but why should a vessel leave a port without clearance? I can see no reason, except that there might be some reason in the master's mind. If he wants to hide the character of his cargo he may well wish to leave without a clearance. It may be no very serious thing to pass the immigration border without reporting. It is a technical offence to go across without reporting, but there is the provision disqualifying the one who does it from passing freely on the other side if he is caught. It may be no very serious offence in itself to fail to disclose anything he should declare in regard to goods that he is bringing in, but I submit that if he fails to go through the form provided by the government in reference to the clearing of goods then he comes under the law. In this particular case it seems to me it is the bounden duty of every master to take a clearance, so that we are not going further than we did in the other case if we say that the failure to take a clearance ought to be considered prima facie evidence that there is something wrong; and if we went as far as we did in the other case we would place the burden of proof on the master of the vessel. I am not saying it is fair, but that is what we did in the other instance. Of course, compared with the advantage that may be gained by the party if he gets his cargo through, the fine of $1,000 is a mere bagatelle.
In the evidence produced last year it was made clear that the traffic in liquor was at the bottom of the whole trouble. I do not think there can be any doubt of that.
Very largely.

In view of that fact it
seems to me we should impose a severe penalty in a case of this kind. I am not familiar with the methods by which the business is carried on, or with the distinction which has been drawn between the two matters referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver
Customs Act Amendment

Centre. It seems to me that even with this provision it would be quite possible for a man who wanted to leave with a cargo of liquor to do so, and considering the amount of the fine he might very well be tempted to do so and refuse to obtain clearance papers, apart altogether from the question of bonding. It would still be possible for a man to leave our shores with a cargo of illegal liquor, even with a fine of $1,000.
Make it $2,000.
Yes, any amount.
Suppose the boat had a collision in port and got out in order to avoid a fine, do you think the owner should pay $1,000?
You can rake up all kinds of exceptional cases, but we cannot give consideration to those. The jpenalty is not adequate and it should be adequate.
What part of the section does my hon. friend refer to when he says the penalty is not adequate?
If the vessel has a cargo of spirituous liquor.
I move that it be amended and that the amount be fixed at $2,000.
Make it $5,000, if you like.
Carried.

The first part of the clause is more important than the second part. The first part deals with the vessel leaving port without a clearance. Not long ago such an act would be taken as prima facie evidence of piracy and a vessel leaving without a clearance would have to pay the penalty.

That applies not merely to vessels that might be suspected of smuggling liquor, but to any vessels. It must be remembered that, in the matter of clearances the Customs department has control, although to my mind it would be better if the granting of clearances were under some other department. In the case of small local vessels going out every few days, the master gets careless and does not report and the idea in imposing a $400 fine in the first part of the clause is simply to discipline the vessel. The latter part of the clause would apply to that class whom we suspect of practising smuggling as a business-illegal operation. There is that distinction. It is an anomaly which should not exist in this act, but it has been there from time immemorial.

There is a difference between the two classes of shipping, and I suggest that this section be held over and reframed. The language is not sufficient. With reference to vessels leaving port without a clearance, there is the further offence of delivering a report of false content, and you are going to let the offender get away with a fine of $400.
That has been the law for thirty years.

Conditions and times have changed in the last thirty years. Thirty years ago there were no motor cars on the road, no radio, no commercial smuggling between the two countries and no reason for it, and to say that it was in the law twenty or thirty years ago is no reason why it should not be changed now to meet present conditions.

I would suggest to the minister that it might be advisable to withdraw the section at t)he moment. I have reference to the last two lines-
And the vessel shall be detained in any port in Canada until the said penalty is paid.
How can she be detained after the owner, has committed the offence and the vessel has sailed away?

It seems to me the point in regard to the clearing of vessels is not well understood. It does not apply to a vessel leaving Canada. It applies to the coastwise trade, vessels going from one port to another, and this committee does not want to impose extreme penalty on vessels doing a coastwise trade. If hon. members understood what this means to the shipping trade they would consider that this section was sufficient to meet the case. It is simply disciplinary. This very act has been in force since 1896, and in my experience in administering the customs laws of this country I have made many detentions where the captains neglected to clear their vessels in the coastwise trade, or even vessels clearing from one port in Canada with a part cargo to another port and leaving without a clearance. In those cases we have to detect them when they reach the other port in Canada before they finally go to sea. So really the penalty in the first part of this clause should not be increased; but where a vessel has liquor on board and the captain makes a false declaration to the collector of customs, he is guilty of perjury, for which the penalty should be severe. If the act is not enforced there will be all kinds of abuses,

Customs Act Amendment
specially in the coastwise trade, and the customs authorities will lose control of those vessels.
I appreciate what the Postmaster General says about the difficulty of routine clearances, but this to my mind is a further reason why the clause should be redrafted.
We have had it for many years without any mistakes occurring.
Then why change it?
Only where the cargo is composed of liquor is there any change.

Everyone who has lived on the seacoast knows that vessels have to have routine clearances, but I do not think any argument adduced so far should convince the committee that the section should be passed. I ask that it be held over.
Does the minister consider that a fine of four hundred dollars is an adequate penalty for a roaster who "delivers a false content, or does not truly answer the questions demanded of him"?

That is not the only penalty imposed. Clause 254 of the Customs Act reads as follows:
Every person who forges, counterfeits falsifies. or uses when so forged, counterfeited or falsified, any paper or document required under this act, or for any purpose therein mentioned, whether written, printed or otherwise, or by any false statement procures such document, knowing the same to be forged, counterfeited or falsified, or forges, counterfeits or falsifies any certificate relating to any oath or declaration or affirmation by this act required or authorized, is guilty of an indictable offence.
Under which clause would the department act?
Both.
