speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment moved by the Postmaster General, that the word "one" in the twentieth line be struck out and the word "two" substituted, carry?

Before the section passes I
want to call attention to a phase which has not been mentioned to-night, and which I think is wrong. I know I will be told that it is nothing new, but I do not know that age particularly lends authority to an absurdity. The section reads that the master of any vessel who having received a clearance-perhaps he has liquor on board and has a legal clearance-goes out and takes in tow another vessel or performs any work without having mentioned in the report outwards his intention so to do, he is liable to a penalty of two thousand dollars. That is, he is supposed before he goes out to state that it is his intention to take a vessel in tow. He sees a small steamer or a gasoline boat in distress, takes it in tow, and for that act of humanity he is liable to a penalty of two thousand dollars or four hundred dollars.
No.

I suppose someone will say that that penalty would never be enforced, but I think the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) will bear me out when I say that not long ago a Canadian boat going down the coast with liquor and away outside the legal limit of American control took a dozen or so men off a vessel in distress, and ran into the nearest port to land them, which of course brought her into American waters. Thereupon the master and crew were put in gaol for having liquor on board in American territorial waters. Here is a situation somewhat similar. Unless the captain knows beforehand that he is going to encounter rough weather, and to go to the rescue of a boat in distress he is liable to a penalty of two thousand dollars, simply for exercising the ordinary humanity of seamen. Would it not be possible to adjust that absurdity, or at least for the minister to give me an explanation?

The section applies only
within the three mile limit in Canadian waters. We have no jurisdiction beyond.

My hon. friend will understand that this section would not apply in the case of a vessel helping another in distress. Here is the point in the tow. A tug might get its clearance for, say, Vancouver to Nanaimo and pick up a scowload of liquor. If the captain gets a clearance for the purpose of taking a tow, he is bound to so state. If, however, he wants to evade the excise law by taking in tow a cargo of liquor on a scow out in the gulf in order to land it further down the coast, he comes clearly within the act. My good friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) is better versed in this than I am, but I think he will assure the hon. member that where a vessel picks up another in distress the Canada Shipping Act will amply cover the case.
Would it not be easy to insert "except in case of distress"?
Yes, but I do not think it necessary.

We have rough water and
boats in distress within the three mile limit.
Customs Act Amendment
la a case of this kind on whom is to be the burden of proof that the vessel was in distress?

I should like the Minister of Customs to declare whether the three mile limit means three nautical miles or three land miles. I ask the question for the benefit of the present member for Antigonish-Guysborough.
Oh, oh.
Three marine miles.
Understand that?

It looks to me as if you are
within the three miles yourself to-night.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On Section 30-Contravention generally- forfeiture.

Mr. Chairman, I [DOT] understand that if a man smuggles goods into this country in an old secondhand Ford car he is liable to lose his car, but if he uses a high powered Studebaker-which the rum runner generally does-he is not liable to have his car forfeited. Is that correct?

I am informed that that
is not correct. I do not know on what the inference is based.

It is quite plain:
All goods shipped or unshipped, imported or exported, carried or conveyed, contrary to this act or to any regulation made by the Governor in Council, and all goods or vehicles, and all vessels under the value of four hundred dollars, with regard to which the requirements of this act or any such regulation have not been complied with, shall be forfeited and may be seized.
Then follows the next section.
Mr. McLean (Melfort):	The argument
of my hon. friend from Weyburn is reasonable. A man smuggling goods in a vessel valued at S400 is liable to have his whole cargo seized. But a high powered car comes along-

A car is not a
vessel.

The section
provides that all goods shipped or unshipped, imported or exported, and all goods or vehicles and all vessels under the value of $400, shall be seized.

The comma
comes after vehicles. The "value of $400" applies to the vessels.
It seems to me that if you forfeit the whole thing in one case you ought to forfeit all in the other.

Section agreed to.
On section 31-If vessel is of value of $400 master liable to penalty of $400.

The minister
may be glad to have his attention drawn to the fact that he may seize the vessel and exact its full value under this section.
We may seize the vessel now under another clause.

Only three words are
being changed in this section. This is tried legislation which has been in use for years.

Section agreed to.
On section 32-Contravention of act in other respects.

This section
should stand over. There may be minor offences for which a man might be sent to gaol under this* section and I do not think we should dispose of it without further consideration.

It is the same clause as in
the Excise Act.

Section agreed to.
On section 33-Bribes.

The officer who accepts the
bribe gets five years; the poor fellow who smuggles $200 worth of goods gets seven years. I just want to point that out.

We should not necessarily impose imprisonment. That should be left to the discretion of the judge. In some cases men have been sent to gaol without the option of a fine when in my opinion it should have been left to the judgment of the court to decide upon an alternative. It might be a serious thing to impose the penalty of imprisonment without the option of a fine.

Section agreed to.
Sections 34 to 36 inclusive agreed to.
On section 37-Counsel fee.

What is the
explanation of this section?

The explanation is given
on the opposite page.

The section
provides for "a reasonable counsel fee in the discretion of the court." Why enact that there shall be any counsel fee?

Customs Act Amendment

Would this "reasonable
counsel fee" be 1200 a day plus $20 a day expenses, as in the case of the customs inquiry? Would that be a reasonable fee?

It is left to the discretion
of the court.

Section agreed to.
On section 38-Minimum penalty.

If there is one section worse than another in this bill it is section 38. I shall not discuss subsection 1 for the moment, but subsection 2 reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Criminal Code or any other statute or law, the court, in a case of the conviction of any person charged with an indictable offence under this act, shall have no power to suspend sentences.
The reason as given in the explanation is that the proposal is intended to meet the situation which has arisen in prosecutions for indictable offences, where the accused has been committed for trial and the prosecution is conducted by the local crown attorney, who is not under the control of this department; the accused, having been found guilty, has been allowed his liberty on suspended sentence, contrary to the opinion and desire of the department. The judge hears the case, knows all its circumstances and, has had the accused before him. He is appointed by the highest authorities to administer the law and to give justice to all the citizens of this country and may decide in his wisdom that sentence may be suspended. Because of that fact and because an official located in the department at Ottawa, who knows nothing of the case and nothing of the circumstances surrounding it, thinks the judge should have imposed a heavy sentence, we are to change the whole system of law enforcement in this country; we are to take away from properly appointed judges the right to exercise mercy and suspend sentence. If there is anything more ridiculous I cannot find it on the statute books of this country, and I wish again to call the attention of the minister to the situation that will be created. Let us suppose that a man endeavours to cross the international border with half a dozen packages of cigarettes in his pocket or, as I said before, three or four pairs of silk stockings, he gets into an argument with the customs official and during the argument shoots and kills him. For the crime of smuggling the onus of proof is upon him; he must go to gaol; the judge cannot suspend sentence upon him, and he has all the forces of the law arrayed against 32049-98
him. For the crime of murder, for taking the life of his fellow man, he has first of all a preliminary investigation, during which he is given every chance. Then he goes before the grand jury, where a true bill must be found against him; from there he goes before a petty jury, where he must ibe declared guilty by his peers. In addition to that he has the opportunity of appeal, and he is not obliged to go into the witness box to give evidence on his own behalf. Under this law in every case in which the onus of proof is against him he must necessarily go into the witness box and give evidence and be at the mercy of the crown attorney, who may cross-examine him and rake up all the details of his past life. I think the condition would be intolerable. Under conditions such as these we will have police surveillance to an extent unknown m any of the countries of Europe. We have always boasted of the freedom of the individual, and I do not think this is the time to take away that freedom.

Since this clause has some
relation to the other clauses which were disputed, I would suggest that it stand together with the others.
Section stands.
On section 39-Distribution of proceeds.
I would like to ask first of all as to the present practice in regard to this matter?

The practice at present
followed is that informers receive rewards only where there are actual proceeds resulting from the seizure or sale of goods seized. Very frequently goods are destroyed as for instance in the seizure of liquors; these goods may be entirely destroyed, and there will be no proceeds from the seizure. In cases of that kind the informer does his work but receives ' no reward whatever. That is unfair, and this change is intended to correct that.

I do not like
that clause at all; it is outrageous. Every man who informs and gets someone else arrested and fined will be given a part of the fine.

A part of the seizure, but
not of the fine.

You are going
to reward him for finding some one else guilty.	! I ..'I.:

Customs Act Amendment

The minister says the
reward does not come out of the fine, but the section says:
Prescribing the manner in which the proceeds of penalties and forfeitures shall be distributed-
The word "penalties" covers a fine, surely.
No.

It may mean the double
duty.

In connection with the distribution of proceeds there is a matter I would like to bring to the attention of the minister; it does not fall entirely within this section, but perhaps it is covered more completely here than in any other section. In the case of an indictable offence a preliminary investigation is first held, and then the charge is laid or an indictment is preferred against the individual. In some instances men are kept in gaol for perhaps months before their case is heard, and during the time they are in gaol the expense of keeping them must be borne by the municipality in which they happen to be arrested, I have in mind one particular case which occurred in the county of Lunenburg some time ago; a vessel called the Ellice B was seized and five men were kept in gaol four or five months at the expense of the county. These cases are not exceptional; they are becoming more frequent every year, and it seems to me some provision should be made for the payment of a portion of the fines to the municipalities, at least in cases of indictable offences where a fine is also imposed. If witnesses are subpoenaed their fees must be paid by the municipality; the crown attorney is paid by the provincial government and the federal government which initiates the charge pays nothing except the fee of the special counsel who may be engaged. I would very much appreciate some expression in this connection from the minister.

I would like to have some
statement from the minister as to the meaning of the word "informer." Certain facts have come to my notice lately in this connection, and I would like the minister to tell me exactly what is meant.

The informer is the man
upon whose information a conviction is secured or a seizure made.
Is the informer an official of the government, or may he be anyone at all?
Anyone.

It seems to me that that
is rather a vicious principle to adopt even in enforcing the customs laws of this country; it makes everyone a possible informer against his neighbour and I think a practice of that kind should not be recognized. I would far rather let the department have a larger preventive service of its own than to depend on outside information to secure convictions. A certain case came to my notice within the last few weeks of a person who was an informer; he did certain work for the preventive force of the Customs department. The same individual happens to be in gaol for doing the work of the Customs department. 1 have not much sympathy for that particular individual, but at the same time I do not think the government ought to put themselves into a position where their own informers are sent to gaol because they are doing the secret work of the government. Would it not be possible to cut out altogether this particular clause, so that if any information is required the officials of the department can go out themselves and secure it; that no rewards be given to informers but that proper wages be given to departmental officials?

It is a long established
practice that rewards must be given if you are going to obtain information which will convict smugglers. It is perhaps offensive to most of us that men should be spying upon their fellowmen and so on, but it seems to be the only way in which you can obtain the necessary information in order to cope with the evil. The customs officials themselves cannot be informers and we have to depend upon others to supply us with information in connection with smuggling. Any seizures that are made or convictions that are obtained bring to the informer a certain reward. I admit at once the profession is not a particularly pleasant one, but it seems to be necessary in order to enable us to carry out the law properly.
Has the minister any information to give to the committee as to how this works out in actual practice?
I can merely say in a general way that it is found fairly successful.

If you do not do that you
have to have an organized secret service which would cost the country a good deal of money.

Can the minister give me
an answer to the question I asked) with reference to the policy of his department as to allowing municipalities, which are responsible

Customs Act Amendment
for keeping the peace and have to bear a large share of the expenses in connection with these prosecutions, to obtain some portion of the proceeds from the fines?

I regret very much that I
cannot give my hon. friend a definite reply except to say I am informed that I have no jurisdiction in the matter.

I would like an
explanation from the minister of a couple of lines in paragraph (n) which reads:
Prescribing the manner in which the proceeds of penalties and forfeitures shall be distributed

The new part reads:
-and providing for payment to informers forthwith after seizure of an award based upon the value of the goods seized and not dependent upon forfeiture or proceeds of forfeiture.
I agree that the minister must have efficient help in order to enforce the law, but I do not understand the wisdom of giving informers payments based upon the value of goods seized' forthwith after seizure, and not dependent upon whether those goods have been forfeited or not. If informers are going to be rewarded for simply going out and seizing, they will continue to do that and the department will get into serious trouble. If, as is quite possible, this depends upon seizure and conviction, I would suggest that the words "and conviction" be added1 after the word "seizure" in order to make this paragraph plhin.

I may interject here that this was one of the very difficult problems with which we were faced last year. The sentiment expressed by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was, I think, entertained by every member of the committee on the first approach of this problem, but we examined with care the officers of the department and this question was carried along for some weeks. The final decision was expressed in this clause in the report:
The committee recommends that the regulation governing the distribution of proceeds of fines and forfeitures be revised and that more liberal treatment be accorded informers and seizing officers.
The point referred to in this clause arose out of the situation. Very frequently as a result of information a seizure is made that is of distinct value to the country. I could cite many and illustrate some striking ones. Then for some reason or another the seizure is not immediately wound up, or a case may occur where the goods are of such a character that they are destroyed. For instance, let us take one of the most difficult things that the country is facing and has faced for years- 32649-98$
narcotic drugs. If a seizure is made of narcotic drugs of considerable value, such seizure perhaps entailing on the part of the informer the greatest risk of any class of his work, those goods are destroyed; there is no return from them. The goods cannot be sold and a moiety given to the informer. Therefore this provides that in a case of that character the department, or the government, or the country, will pay to the informer a moiety proportionate to the value of those goods had they been sold instead of being destroyed, although it is distinctly in the interests of the country that the goods be destroyed. That is the reason for this amendment. I may add, as I said in my opening remarks, that I agree with all those who have a dislike for moieties to informers, or stool pigeons, or whatever you like to call them. All my life I have had an abhorrence of this practice. On the other hand there are many, I was going to say very respectable individuals who act as informers although there are many who are certainly far from respectable.

Do those people who are
respectable do the work for the benefits that accrue from it?
Yes, some of them make a profession of it.
Just as a detective does.

They are practically
private detectives, if you like. I am not saying that it is a profession one would glorify at all, but it is one of those lines of business that is followed and that is seemingly very necessary in order properly to detect crime.

I have no objection to the informer being rewarded for his services, but what I object to and what I would like to get the minister to explain is the part of the paragraph which reads:
And providing for payment to informers forthwith after seizure of an award based upon the value of the goods seized.
I appreciate the hon. member's explanation as far as it has gone in regard to goods that are destroyed. It is in the interests of the country that such goods should be destroyed; they cannot be sold. But if this is left as it is and the words "and conviction" are not added after the word "seizure", it is going to lead to criminals getting together, one of them acting as informer for the Customs department, another coming along with the goods and having them seized, his partner being rewarded and he himself appealing to the court and getting the goods released. This
Customs Act Amendment

clause like many others in the bill is not worded so that the ordinary layman can understand what it means.

Does my hon. friend know that section 286 of the act gives the governor in council power to make regulations? This is not a statutory amendment; it is the power to make regulations to cover such cases.
Mr. MoLEAN (Melfort): The copy of the bill which I have reads:
Paragraph (n) of section 286 of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor.

I have a copy of the act, and section 286 reads:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, and in the manner hereinafter provided, in addition to the other purposes and matters in this act mentioned, make regulations for or relating to the following purposes and matters.
Is there anything unreasonable, in adding after the word "seizure" the words "and conviction"?
It still remains in the discretion of the government to make such regulations as it sees fit to deal with the situation.
This is giving them power without a conviction having been registered.
It gives them power, but it does not make it obligatory upon them to do so.
What is the objection to adding the words "and conviction"?
There are lots of seizures and forfeitures without convictions; that is the trouble.
With regard to the new and respectable class of civil servants which the acting minister of customs-
That is not the language that I used.

The acting minister spoke of somewhat respectable informers. In view of his experience with the operation of the law, which apparently will be confided to his care, I think it would be well for him to organize that service, because, after all, what with those informers who are respectable, those who are not respectable, and those who are ordinary criminals and are going to partake with respectable criminals in some of the receipts of the Customs department, we should go a step further, I suppose, and have them classified by the Civil Service Commission. Those of them who are respectable, since the government and the laws of the

land are going to encourage this kind of administration, should be put on the regular civil service list and a part of their proceeds should go to the pension fund, so that we might create in the land that kind of cooperation in the public service. Since it is found that the police force of the Customs department is not capable of dealing with the law and enforcing the penalties, since it is found that the ordinary principles of law as applied from time immemorial are not sufficient for the trial of individuals violating this law, since we are creating this new legislation for the correction of this enormous crime of smuggling, I would suggest that we make this new form of civil service an effective one.
Get a classification by the commission.

Yes, and ratings and all that sort of thing which the Civil Service Commission does. That might help to stimulate the ordinary service of this department which is found to be totally ineffective for the application of the law. Really, seriously speaking, Mr. Chairman, I think it is most shameful that in a public law it should be declared that we offer a reward to one of the most contemptible and despicable classes of people. It may be necessary in war for generals to make use of spies. They may be obliged at times to bribe individuals belonging to the other army to get information; but I have never heard that it was considered that the spying process with which war is accompanied is acknowledged by law and rewarded by law, and of parliament voting the money. As far as I am concerned this whole clause is revolting to every sense of decency. It is all very well to pass laws to please a certain number of merchants in Montreal, Toronto, and elsewhere, to help them against the small smugglers, though we have been helping them for years past in the kind of smuggling they are carrying on themselves by false entries given to the regular officers of the customs service, as has been done from time immemorial, in Montreal at least, that I know of. It is all very well to pass extraordinary laws, drastic laws, immoral laws to help a small and powerful class of people who were evidently able to impose their will upon the last government and upon the present branch office of the Tory government; but at the same time as a Canadian and as a liberal-minded representative of the people I protest against such kind of legislation.

It is most interesting to hear the protest of my hon. friend with that facility of language he has for clothing his

Customs Act Amendment
insinuations, but I would like to remind the House and the committee that this law that he talks about has been on the statute books for a great many years: indeed, it was originated and passed when he was a younger member of this House by the government of which he was then a supporter. I am discussing this subject as a member of the House, and I intend to exercise my right to discuss legislation without asking the hon. gentleman's permission to do so. I am taking this amendment as an amendment to an act that has been in force for a great many years. I took the opportunity of saying a moment ago to the committee that this whole subject, which is repugnant, I will admit, to practically all of us, was analyzed and discussed by the committee. We did the best we could to find some other solution for this method of detecting crime, but no other solution presented itself than the one that is presented here. It has been in the law since 61 Victoria, 62 and 63 Victoria., and 3 Edward VII. This amendment is merely adding a very few words. It is not introducing any new principle: it is no new departure from the law at all. It merely provides that where the goods seized produce no return, the informer in that case shall receive a moiety equal to the value of the goods or to the portion of the goods which would have come to him had they been sold.
There is not much occasion at this stage of the game to heap abuse either upon the minister or upon myself or others who may support his efforts to meet, a very difficult situation. Let me add this. The whole country realized when the hon. gentleman took office as Minister of Customs that he was undertaking a very, very serious task. I wrote him a letter which he has on his file, when I left the office, tendering to him then my cooperation in making this department effective and efficient. Not only that, but I have offered him my cooperation across the floor of this House, and I think it ill behooves my hon. friend from Labelle to throw a few cheap slights at me because I am tendering to the minister the benefit of what little experience I may have had in this matter and what little support I can give him in getting this very difficult legislation through. No minister has as heavy a task as the Minister of National Revenue. His department has grown into an enormous one. A few years ago it was only the Customs department. What has he got to-day? Customs, all of the excise, which was a separate department when I came into this House, all of the sales tax. the income tax,
and all the stamp taxes. He has more responsibility and a greater burden upon his shoulders than any other minister. In addition to that, beoause of circumstances which we will not analyze now, he found when he entered the department that it had, according to a report of a committee of this House, largely broken down. Without now making any recriminations as to why it broke down, the fact is there, and the minister is now trying to lift this department into some efficient state of organization. I am here to help him; I will give him my help to the best of my ability, and no clever, cheap quips on the part of my hon. friend from Labelle will intimidate me. I am not the Minister of Customs; I was for a short time, and I will give to the Minister of Customs the benefit of whatever experience and knowledge I have of this very, very difficult and perplexing problem.

The hon. gentleman is quite mistaken if he thinks I want to have any cheap quips at his expense. On the contrary, I congratulate him that he still governs the Department of Customs, and that he has found a very devoted deputy and supporter in the present instance.
My hon. friend is not sincere in that, and he knows it.

I am not criticising at all the efforts that are being made to improve the administration of this department. The efforts that are being made to correct the administration of the department meet with the hearty cooperation of hon. gentlemen opposite. I have no objection to that either. I am simply saying that some of the provisions in this bill have been evidently worded and introduced with the desire to respond at any cost to the feeling that smuggling is the worst and the most abominable offence that can be committed, and also to please the interests of a certain class of people; and under that feeling we are simply forgetting some of the basic principles of legislation and public morality. That is my contention.
With regard to this very section, the hon. member says it is a mere repetition of the previous law. I think that is a false position, because on the opposite page, paragraph (n), we find the law as it stood:
(n) Prescribing the manner in which the proceeds of penalties and forfeitures shall be distributed.
That was the law.
And is the law to-day.

Plus exactly what I denounced, what did not exist before.
Customs Act Amendment

No, my hon. friend is
wrong.

I beg your pardon. The text goes on:
The words underlined in the new paragraph are added.
And these words are:
-and providing for payment to informers forthwith after seizure on an award based upon the value of the goods seized and not dependent upon forfeiture or proceeds of forfeiture.
So that the new words being added now are the official recognition of those informers.
Not at all
Of course they are.

The principle of paying
informers is in the act now and has been there for thirty yeans.
I am not discussing that.
That is the whole point.

I quite admit-we are forced to admit-that in certain operations of government and in the application of laws, ministers are bound at times to resort to certain processes which are repugnant. I compared the fact that informers were being used with the fact that at times spies have been used. But I objected to having informers brought into the law as regular servants of the government and paid by the government out of public funds.

They are used no more
now than they were formerly.

Yes, I beg pardon. In former times the minister could make use of them and pay them, but there was not an acknowledged system in the law of employment of informers, emphasized by the declaration of the minister that in all cases his officials accept information from anybody, from that class of respectable informers of whom the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has spoken, as well as from any scalawag or any criminal, who will now be placed in a position to exercise vengeance or blackmail most powerfully and will be able to place the whole burden of proof upon his victim. The judge will have no discretion in the matter and will have to take the evidence as it is made by the informer-respectable or non-respectable, criminal or otherwise, perjurer, perhaps, who will be the paid agent of the government of Canada, who will be offered a recompense by the government of Canada, and the judge will have to convict the victim who may be more innocent than the paid agent of the government acting under this law.

Which has been in the
law and has been the practice for thirty years.

Then we are in the face of a falsification; because the text of the law simply states that the minister may pass regulation to direct how the proceeds of the siezure will be distributed; but unless this is a falsification the informers were not acknowledged in the law and were not paid by the law. It was a discretionary power in the hands of the government to distribute the proceeds of the seizure as it is worded here:
Prescribing the manner in which the proceeds of penalties and forfeitures shall be distributed.
In other words it was a discretionary power exercised under a law far less rigid than the present provision and far less drastic.
No.
I beg pardon.

My hon. friend will not
argue that the adding of these words, which merely provide that in case the goods forfeited are not sold they can be provided for in the way prescribed here, is giving any more powrnr in the distribution of moieties than is in the original act.
Why add them?

For the very reason that
in some cases goods are not realized upon, and this is to provide that in such cases the moiety may be paid.

Under the text of the
law as it stood there was no legal recognition of the services of the informer.
Yes, there was.

There was discretionary power given to the minister to distribute the proceeds of the seizure, and under that discretionary power his officials could reward the informer, but that was all. If the discretionary power given is all that is being asked for, why add these words? However, in a sense it is better to have it that way; because that shows the spirit of this new law, to be carried on against all principles of legislation and administration as applied in civilized countries.

I would like to endorse what my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has said. This section is revolting in the extreme. To my mind the whole thing is revolting. We have been trying to-night to legislate for the administration of an act that is an evil in itself. In common with my hon.

Customs Act Amendment
friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I do not mind saying frankly to this House that I have always taken the stand that protection is not only economically wrong, but that it is morally wrong. In this bill to-night we have differentiated between one evil and another. The man who brings goods into this country is liable under this measure to fine and imprisonment and his goods are liable to seizure. When the people defy the law by exercising what should be the inalienable right of citizens to buy and sell where they please, the utmost penalty is incurred. But when a cargo of liquor is sent out from a port without the captain securing a proper clearance, what is the penalty? We send that liquor out to demoralize the citizens and defy the laws of a friendly country, and *we impose a $1,000 fine upon the offender, which to him is not more than ten cents to the ordinary man. The whole thing is immoral, the law is immoral. The act we are putting through to-night is an indictment against the nation. This very section is nothing more than the crowning act of an evil law, and is revolting in the extreme.

I should like to
test the feeling of the House. It seems to me that this particular practice is abhorrent to the good sense of all the members who have spoken on the section. I do not believe we are justified in encouraging other people to do what we ourselves would refuse to do. Let me quote the explanatory note:
Informers, particularly with regard to offences against the liquor laws, take great risks of property and even life, and it is believed that if prompt awards could be paid as provided by this amendment the receiving of information would be facilitated.
This simply means that if we put up a larger reward we encourage those unfortunate individuals to take greater "risks of property and even life." In my own city a few years ago the police magistrate refused to take the evidence of informers, and their use was finally abandoned because it was found to encourage men who were essentially criminal in character. Therefore I move:
That all the words after the word "repealed" in the nineteenth line to the word "forfeiture" in the twenty-sixth line be struck out.
It simply means deleting paragraph (n).

In reply to the remarks
made by the hon. member for Labelle, I do not think any new principle is being introduced by recognizing in terms an informer and the payment to him of a certain portion of the penalty. This is recognized in our Criminal Code in express terms in section 1041 and 1042. They provide that a moiety
of any penalties imposed shall belong to the informer or person who sues for the same, and the other moiety to His Majesty for the public uses of Canada. I quite realize in common with other members that the informer engages in a rather undesirable job, but I do not think we are going outside our legislative purview in this instance. We are simply providing that whereas now the informer is paid only a portion of the penalty after the conviction, new regulations may be made under which he may be paid an amount based on the value of the goods seized.

There is a radical
difference between the case quoted by the hon. minister and this case. The former is a rather rare type of case and is surrounded by all the protection afforded to the accused person under the criminal law; but here you disregard all the principles incident to the trial of an accused person. You put him in the most unfavourable position with respect to the burden of proof and the discretion of the court, so that he can hardly defend himself ; and then, having discarded all the guarantees given to the accused before he is found guilty, you invite thousands of individuals from the Pacific to the Atlantic to interest themselves in the application of this law in order to make money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the government has been making an honest effort to correct some of the abuses which were hrought so forcibly to the attention of the House last year, and is quite sincere in its desire to stop smuggling. But it is now twenty minutes to midnight, we have been debating this question for over an hour and apparently the committee are somewhat divided. I for one feel that we have done a pretty good day's work, and I am going to ask my colleague the Minister of Customs to report progress. Probably on reflection hon. members will realize the propriety of the clause as presented.

Mr. Chairman, my hon.
friend the Minister of Finance who is now leading the House says that the government has a sincere intention of passing this bill and improving the customs law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The bill was presented with the sincere desire of putting a stop to smuggling.

He will realize that the
objections to the bill have not emanated from the Conservative opposition. We on this side have used every effort to assist the passage of this measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We recognize that.
The reason it has not been passed1 is that hon. members opposite, supporters of the government, dbjeoted.

Mr. Chairman, I resent what has been said from this side of the House that this measure is fathered or assisted or initiated by anj'one on the other side. The charge is not fair. The language used by the hon. member for Labelle that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is the acting minister of customs is not worthy of the generosity of the race from which he comes.
Hear, hear.

I am not going into the
merits any more than to say that no new principle whatever is introduced in this clause. The informer has always been recognized. It is merely an effort to carry out the recommendations made by the parliamentary committee last session. The opposition that has developed is more or less of a surprise to me. I beg to move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
